items.title: Jack Teagarden Interview, 1959-10-29
items.q: And then I went with, uh, Benny Pollock. ... There was a little kid with us, uh, the name of Benny Goodman. In those days he was about 18 years old. Jimmy McPartland and, uh, Bud Freeman. ... We went to the Park Central Hotel. We stayed there about a year.

ctx.x: Okay, whenever you're ready. Well, how did you learn trombone and develop your style? That's what I really like to know.

Well, I'll tell you, when I was, uh, pretty young, my mother and I used to play in, uh, the old silent movie theaters. We used to play for the comedies and, uh, I don't know, just trombone and piano. You know, learn more technique because I had the whole, swing the whole thing, melody and all. You know. And, uh, my mother played very good ragtime piano, which was very good for those years. Then, uh, I lost my father in 1918 with the flu. And then I went, we went to Oklahoma City. And I went one more year of, uh,…

Can we back up for a minute and go back to your early period? Yeah. Because there's some particular people I'd like to ask you about some particular things. What kind of training did Peg Kelly have that he should develop this wonderful style?

items.title: 66100_Bud Freeman oral history interview
items.q: In fact, I recorded with Jack just before he died. He hired me for the record date... we had Jack Teagarden... I got an offer then to go with Paul Whiteman... in the band were Jack Teagarden

ctx.x: As most of your musical contemporaries, most of the musicians weren't into anything else.

No, I want to say particularly if I may, that I have tremendous respect for Jack Teagarden and there was a story about him that -- I remember that I was playing with the Pollack band, in New York, and Glenn Miller had given his notice and so Ben said & well, we will be looking for another trombone player to take Glenn's place, and I got a call about 3:00 one morning, one of our nights off and the call was from Pee Wee Russell, and he said, <Bud, about the greatest jazz trombone player in the world is blowing into…

So I went over to hear this great player and Pee Wee was at the bar and we waited about a half hour and there appeared at the door, the speakeasy door, a man with a little cap, a button cap, a corduroy Norfolk suit, shoes -- trousers halfway up his legs -- I can't remember the shoes now -- but anyway, I think they were suede shoes and he had a trombone, not in a case, but in a little velvet bag. He took it out of the bag, put it together and played with no accompaniment, some of the finest music I ever have heard…
